energy_field:14-11-7.heading: A steady pace that goes the distance
paragraphs: The overall tone here is set by measure. In what you do, Temperance is at work: you don’t grab at everything at once but pour effort from one thing into another — a bit of work, a bit of rest, a hard task mixed in with an easy one. Your reserves rest on Strength: your own impulses — haste, irritation, the urge to drop it all — you don’t crush but gently tame. And your feelings come from the Chariot: what lifts you is the very sense of movement, when every stretch of road you cover is visible.

**You go the distance precisely because you don’t bolt from the start.** A big renovation, a long course of study, a book written over years: others start with a sprint and run out of steam within a month, while you edge forward a little every day. When you want to give it all up, you don’t force yourself but coax yourself along, the way you would coax a stubborn animal. And one day you look back: you have come a long way, and that sense of the road behind you turns out to be the best reward.

The hardest stretches are the ones where no progress is visible. A steady pace and gentle patience are made for a road you can travel; but when everything stalls — you are waiting on someone else’s answer, the decision isn’t yours to make — the Chariot has nothing to grip. The impulse you are used to taming quietly builds up. And one day it breaks out in a lurch that is nothing like you: drop it all, redo it, start again. Then measure returns — and you are left wondering where that storm came from.

energy_field:14-11-16.heading: An even rhythm and sudden insights
captions: Holding the storm in your hands
paragraphs: From the outside, your life runs at an even pace. That is Temperance in your affairs: work, home and rest are blended so that none of them swallows the others, and the tempo changes gradually. Your staying power comes from Strength: you don’t suppress strong impulses but take them in hand and calm them. Your feelings, though, follow the law of the Tower — not gradually but in a flash. In a single moment it becomes clear that a familiar structure was standing on false foundations.

**Your calm is not the absence of storms but the ability to live through a collapse without wrecking your whole way of life.** Say it turns out that a project you believed in was built on empty promises. Inside, everything comes down in one evening, yet the next morning you still make the coffee, go to the meeting, do what was planned. An even rhythm doesn’t soften the blow, but it gives you a place where you can calmly sort through the rubble and decide what to build again.

The weak spot is that you calm the warning signs too. A small irritation, something that doesn’t add up, a strange remark from someone — all of it is carefully diluted and put aside so as not to break the rhythm. The signals pile up unnoticed until one day everything gives way at once: “That’s it, I’ve had enough.” For the people close to you it comes out of a clear blue sky — everything looked so calm. And what could have been talked through piece by piece now has to be sorted out among the ruins.

energy_field:14-12-8.heading: A pause before a fair decision
paragraphs: You rarely need to run to be on time. Temperance shows in the way you take things on: effort is measured out to the task, work alternates with breathing spaces, and different activities are mixed in a comfortable proportion. Your energy comes from the Hanged Man — from stopping: as soon as you step out of the race for a while and look at everything from the other side, the strength for the next step appears. And you live through events by way of Justice: you feel at ease when things are fair, and weighed down when the accounts don’t balance.

**You don’t rush to a conclusion — and that is why your conclusion is usually fair.** Say some friends are arguing about how to split the costs of a holiday cottage they share. You don’t answer in the heat of the moment: you take a pause, look through each person’s eyes, work out who uses the place how often and who has put how much into it. A couple of days later you bring a breakdown in which nobody feels short-changed. The pause turns out to be not a delay but part of the work.

The difficulty comes when the pause drags on because there is no fair solution. Some situations have no exact measure, and any choice will hurt someone. Then you keep hanging between the options: weighing, looking from yet another side, waiting for the scales to tip by themselves. Meanwhile things run at half speed, and an awkwardness builds inside, as if it were your fault that you can’t decide fairly. In the end the decision is made by circumstances — and not in the fairest way.

energy_field:14-15-11.heading: A strong pull on a gentle lead
paragraphs: You are driven by strong desire. The Devil explains where your energy comes from overall: from whatever holds you tight — work you love, the thrill of the game, things and people you cling to in earnest. Without that kind of hook, your strength never quite switches on. Temperance sets the outward pace: you don’t throw the pull into action all at once but dilute it and alternate — the evening for the passion, the morning for duties. And in your feelings Strength is at work: you don’t smother a strong emotion but calmly hold it by the mane.

**In you, a strong pull becomes a workhorse, not a master.** Say you have been gripped by a new game, a collection or the idea of a business of your own. Someone else in your place would vanish for a month, while you spread the passion across the week like seasoning across a dish: a little, but every day. The desire doesn’t fade — on the contrary, it feeds everything else: duties go more briskly because your favourite thing is waiting in the evening.

The weak spot is the conviction that everything is under control. Since you manage to dose the pull, it seems safe, and the limits gradually shift: half an hour turns into an hour, “only at weekends” into “and on Wednesdays too”. Strength helps you not notice the tension: you are calm, holding on, no slip-ups. But holding on is effort too, and one day it turns out that most of your energy goes not on your affairs but on keeping a balance with the very thing that holds you.

energy_field:15-8-5.heading: A firm grip and an honest agreement
captions: Holding on to what you start
paragraphs: In practical matters you have a firm grip. That is the Devil in your material rhythm: once you take something on — a job, a renovation, saving up — you hold on tight, with real force, and it is hard to let go of anything unfinished. Justice decides where your strength goes: you share it out by honest accounts — what goes in should come back out. And the Hierophant can be heard in your feelings: you are calmest when life follows an accepted order and important events have a recognised form.

**What you rely on is an agreement that both sides keep.** You are ready to work without days off for a shared goal, provided the rules are clear: who does what, who gets what, how the finish will be marked. Say a family is saving for a home of its own: you keep the spreadsheet of expenses, put something aside from every pay cheque and know that on the day of the purchase everyone will gather round a celebratory table. A pull towards the goal, honest bookkeeping and a shared ritual add up to something others can rely on.

The trouble starts when the agreement stops working but the grip remains. Circumstances have changed, a partner is putting in less, the rules are out of date — yet letting go of what you have invested feels unfair: “so much has gone into this already”. You hold on tighter and insist on an order that no longer helps anyone. The familiar form is soothing, even though there is less and less meaning behind it. A chain once chosen freely turns into an obligation dragged along out of inertia.

energy_field:15-8-14.heading: Absorption that keeps its accounts
paragraphs: When you are busy with something, you mean it. The Devil can be felt in what you do: a task, an object, a project takes hold of you completely, and it is hard to tear yourself away. Justice watches how your strength is shared out: inside you keep a tally of how much goes to work, how much to the people close to you and how much to yourself, and any imbalance is felt at once. And Temperance softens your feelings: joy doesn’t tip into euphoria, disappointment doesn’t tip into despair, and strong emotions are diluted to ones you can live with.

**You can burn with your work without robbing the rest of your life.** Suppose a whole week, evenings included, went on an urgent order. On Saturday you pay back the debt honestly: a whole day with your loved ones, no phone, and the very outing you promised long ago. Inside there is neither panic that everyone has been neglected nor self-satisfaction — just balance restored. The absorbing work stays, but it doesn’t take more than its due.

The danger lies in a balance that is a little too convenient. If every imbalance can be made up for later, the work’s grip quietly tightens: the urgent week becomes the usual one, and “I’ll make it up on Saturday” becomes a habitual promise. Temperance smooths over the unease, and the feeling that something is wrong never gets the chance to sound loudly. On paper the accounts balance, but your loved ones get their weekends on schedule, while your living attention stays wherever the work holds it.

energy_field:15-11-8.heading: Drive that doesn’t cross the line
paragraphs: Your overall tone is strong drive under good supervision. In your affairs the Devil leads: you want a lot and you want it now, and you hold tight to what you have started, what you have earned, your place. Strength provides the energy — the ability to tame your own lion: you feel greed, excitement and irritation, but you don’t let them decide for you. And Justice shapes how outcomes are felt: luck pleases you when it is honest, and a loss is easier to accept when you understand where it came from.

**You want what is yours in earnest — and that is exactly why you make sure not to take what isn’t.** For example, a large bonus is being divided up at work, and you have every reason to fight for a bigger share. And you do fight — persistently, with figures in hand. But at the moment when you could lean on people and take more than your share, something inside stops you. Getting what is yours fairly tastes sweeter to you than winning at any cost.

The vulnerable spot is situations where the accounts can’t be settled fairly. You held yourself back and played by the rules, while someone else pushed through and won. Then the tamed lion starts demanding its due: resentment lasts longer than it should, and you keep recounting in your head who got how much. Holding back gets harder and harder, and one day you want to stop being the one who plays fair. A chain of resentment holds no less tightly than the greed you tamed so skilfully.

energy_field:15-11-17.heading: Carrying a heavy load with hope ahead
paragraphs: The material side of your life is rarely a stroll. The Devil shows in your affairs: you get drawn in seriously — into a big project, a building job, a household — and they hold you tight. Your staying power comes from Strength: you don’t chase away fear and irritation but calmly tame them, so you don’t panic even under pressure. And the Star governs how all this is felt: there is always a light ahead, and after every hard stage comes a sense of renewal.

**You can carry something heavy for a long time because you never lose sight of what it is for.** Say a few years go into a workshop of your own: orders in the evenings, holidays postponed, every expense counted. Some people grow bitter along the way, while you celebrate every satisfied customer as a small holiday and share that hope with the people close to you. The load doesn’t get lighter, but around you it never feels hopeless.

The flip side is that hope can keep you where it is time to leave. “Just a bit longer and it’ll get easier” — that makes it easier to put up with a job that has long been wringing you dry, or an arrangement where you give more than you get. Your calm staying power helps you not notice the chain getting shorter. The light ahead never goes out, but it always stays the same distance away, and the years go on walking towards it rather than living in it.

energy_field:15-14-11.heading: Loving the tangible without being captured
paragraphs: You are drawn to the tangible: good things, good food, comfort, money you can actually hold. The Devil is at work in your affairs: you become attached to whatever brings pleasure straight away, and you act for its sake with real force. Temperance decides how your strength is shared out: you pour it from work into rest and back, mixing the pleasant with the necessary — and that is how you refill. And Strength sounds in your feelings: you don’t scold or suppress temptation but calmly take it in hand.

**For you, pleasure is not the enemy of work but its fuel.** Say a hard week lies ahead. You lay out small treats along it in advance: a favourite lunch on Wednesday, a new book for Friday, a good evening at the end. The work goes more smoothly because every stretch has been sweetened. And when you feel like buying something completely unnecessary, you don’t make a scene with yourself — you simply put the wish off for a day and see whether it is still there.

The risk is that the balance comes to rest on rewards. If every effort has to be sweetened, the rewards grow: a pricier lunch, a bigger purchase, a longer evening. You are still calm and sure you are in charge of the pull — after all, there are no slip-ups. But without the usual treat your strength stops flowing between things: work without a reward seems unbearably bland. Then it is no longer you who hands out the pleasure; the pleasure decides what you are willing to take on.

energy_field:16-8-6.heading: Breaking the false for honest closeness
paragraphs: Your affairs have their breaking points. This is how the Tower shows itself: life goes on in its usual way until it becomes clear that the foundation is false — and then everything changes at once: job, home, the way you live. Justice explains where your strength comes from: from honest accounts, when what you put in matches what you get back, and what is said matches what is done. And the Lovers colour your feelings: the deepest feeling comes beside a person with whom you don’t have to pretend.

**You don’t cling to a way of life if there is no truth in it — and you are ready to rebuild it for the sake of real closeness.** Say a job pays well but requires you to tell people things you don’t believe. One day it becomes clear that you can’t go on like this, and you leave — abruptly, without long hesitation. That evening you tell someone close to you about it and feel not fear but relief: now there is nothing between you that has to be hidden.

The difficulty is that honesty can sound like a verdict. If something in a relationship seems unequal or left unsaid, you want to bring down the whole structure at once rather than take it apart brick by brick. “If that’s how it is, then it was all a lie” — and a shared past is written off in a single evening. The other person may not understand what happened: a moment ago things were warm, and suddenly you are demanding a full reckoning. The collapse looks honest, but some of what was precious goes along with what was false.

energy_field:16-8-15.heading: Breaking with the unfair, yet not letting go
captions: Pulling down what has had its day
Energy from a sense of measure
paragraphs: Your material rhythm can’t stand pretence. The Tower shows in your affairs: if the way your life is set up turns out to rest on a false foundation, you don’t patch the cracks — you knock it down and start again. Justice explains where your strength comes from: from the sense that actions have consequences and everything should be above board. And in your feelings there is the Devil — an attachment that grips hard: to people, to places, to whatever you have put yourself into.

**You make decisions by your conscience and feel with your whole heart — and one doesn’t cancel the other.** Say a business partner has been underpaying you for years, and you end the partnership with a single email. It is the right thing to do, and even freeing. But for a long time afterwards you catch yourself thinking about them, going over your shared successes, missing the good things there were. You can act honestly even when it hurts, and you don’t lose the ability to grow deeply attached.

It is harder when the collapse has happened but the chain is still there. On the outside everything is broken off, but inside the hearing goes on: who was right, who owes whom, what you should have said. Resentment holds no less tightly than the old attachment, and the energy that should have gone into building something new is spent on settling old scores. It can also work the other way: so as not to fall into that kind of dependence again, you are ready to pull down the next connection at the first suspicion of dishonesty.

energy_field:16-10-8.heading: Sharp turns and a fair outcome
paragraphs: Your road is rarely straight. The Tower sets the course of your affairs: familiar structures collapse from time to time, and everything has to be built again — sometimes by your decision, sometimes despite it. The Wheel of Fortune governs your strength: it comes in waves — on the rise you have enough for three, on the downturn only for what matters most. And you live through it all by way of Justice: you need the outcome to match the effort, and other people’s decisions to make sense.

**You know how to start again because you see change not as chaos but as a new turn of the wheel.** Say the company you work for closes, and what took years to build is gone within a week. You don’t get stuck on “why me?” but soberly take stock of what is still rightfully yours: skills, contacts, reputation — earned honestly and not going anywhere. On the next upturn you put all that into something new, and it stands on ground that has already been tested.

The vulnerable spot is wanting to find justice where chance was at work. The wheel doesn’t turn according to merit: someone rises without effort, while a collapse hits you even though you did everything right. Then you want to find out who is to blame, restore the balance, prove your point. While that inquiry goes on, the right moment passes. And resentment at an unfair turn stays with you as a weight that makes it harder to meet the next upturn.

energy_field:16-11-9.heading: Standing firm and finding your own light
paragraphs: Sharp changes are part of your material rhythm. The Tower shows in your affairs: every so often the familiar order collapses, and the rebuilding has to be abrupt, right from the foundations. Strength explains where your energy comes from at such times: you don’t chase away fear and confusion but calmly tame them, without letting them give the orders. And the Hermit can be heard in your feelings: you live through everything important alone with yourself, lantern in hand, until it becomes clear what it all meant.

**You come out of every collapse with an understanding you can later share.** Say a long-held plan falls apart: a move falls through, or a venture you put everything into never gets off the ground. For the first few days you stay steady, deal with what can’t wait and don’t alarm anyone. Then you withdraw into yourself — long walks, silence, notes in a notebook. And a month later you are the one who can calmly tell a friend in a similar mess what helps and what to expect.

The vulnerable spot is solitude that drags on. Coping on your own is so familiar that at the moment of a crash you don’t call anyone: you have the composure, the lion is tamed, the inner lantern is lit. The people close to you find out what happened when it is all over, and may be hurt that they weren’t let in. And sometimes the lantern isn’t enough, and you wander in your thoughts longer than you need to, though someone else’s eyes could have shown you the way out sooner.

energy_field:16-11-18.heading: The courage to walk into the unknown
paragraphs: Life in this tone doesn’t promise a smooth road. The Tower is at work in your affairs: the way they are set up breaks down from time to time, and you rebuild it — sometimes after a blow from outside, sometimes because you yourself have seen the false foundation. Strength gives you energy: you don’t deny fear, but you don’t let it lead either; you soothe it as you would a wild animal. And your feelings move under the Moon: in uncertainty, imagination paints more than can be seen, and anxiety readily tries on the worst outcome.

**You do get frightened — and you keep going anyway, without pretending the fear isn’t there.** For example, after a redundancy you have to look for a new job. At night gloomy scenarios spin in your head; in the morning you sit down and calmly send off your CV, one application after another. Anxiety remains a travelling companion, but not the boss. Over time you learn to recognise its voice, and by that voice alone you can tell: this is imagination, not fact.

Trouble begins when imagination starts predicting the next collapse. If there have been several crashes, it is easy to see a crack where there is none: someone’s silence looks like the beginning of the end, a calm month like the lull before a storm. And then you want to strike first — leave, change, tear down before it falls by itself. Strength helps you stay outwardly steady, so no one sees how much energy goes into fighting ghosts. And sometimes what comes down is something that could have stood perfectly well.

energy_field:16-13-11.heading: Closing chapters with your composure intact
paragraphs: Your changes are never cosmetic. The Tower shows in your affairs: if the way your life is set up no longer matches reality, you don’t touch up the facade — you take the whole structure down. Death explains where your energy comes from: from endings — when a worn-out form goes, room and strength are freed for a new one. And Strength governs your feelings: even at the sharpest turn you keep your composure and meet a loss with courage, without panic.

**You have the courage to admit that a chapter is over and to begin the next one on a clean site.** Say a business you have run for years no longer brings either joy or income. Others would hang on to it out of habit, while you close it down, give away the equipment and say goodbye to your clients. It is sad, but calm. And six months later something is already growing in the freed-up space — something you simply never had the energy for before.

The flip side is a habit of ending things before they have had a chance to come right. If something gets difficult, your hand reaches for the switch of its own accord: it is easier to knock it down and start again than to repair it. And composure gets in the way of living through a loss: you hold yourself so steady that grieving seems to have neither time nor reason. Unmourned losses pile up, and one day yet another ending feels heavier than it should — not because of itself, but because of all the earlier ones you so bravely failed to notice.

energy_field:17-8-7.heading: Generosity with measure and direction
paragraphs: In what you do, you resemble the figure on the Star who pours water from two vessels — onto the land and into the pool. You readily give your time, your skills, your help, and work goes best when it brightens things not only for you. Justice keeps an eye on how your strength is shared out: evenly between the work, the people close to you and yourself, with nothing lopsided. And the Chariot colours your feelings: what pleases you is the sense that everything is moving towards a goal and every step brings it nearer.

**Your generosity doesn’t spill everywhere because it has a measure and a direction.** Say you have offered to help some friends start a small business: you share your experience, your contacts, your evenings. But from the outset you agree how much time you are ready to give and what should be in place by when. Help becomes not an endless rescue mission but a shared road with clear stages — and every stage completed pleases you as much as it pleases them.

The difficulty comes when what you give doesn’t turn into movement. You shared generously and fairly, yet the business stands still: others don’t do their part, deadlines slide, your contribution comes back neither as results nor as thanks. The Chariot hates standing still, and inside you a tally begins: how much has gone in, how much has come back. Generosity that used to flow freely starts being handed out against receipts. Helping gets harder — not because you begrudge it, but because the sense of a road has gone.

energy_field:17-8-16.heading: Openness that won’t forgive pretence
paragraphs: Life is easier for you when there is nothing to hide. The Star sets your way of acting: you share your plans, help without conditions and hope for the best — in people and in things. Justice governs your strength: it is fed by fair exchange, when what you give and what you receive are roughly in balance. And your feelings come by way of the Tower: emotionally, the strongest moment is when a false foundation is suddenly exposed and gives way.

**You build relationships on trust and are ready to see the truth, even if it shatters the picture.** Say you spent years helping a friend and believed the friendship was equal. Then one chance conversation reveals that you are being talked about behind your back. It is a blow, but you don’t hide from it: you admit you were wrong, draw your conclusions and keep the ability to trust — though no longer blindly. The collapse clears space for relationships where what you give comes back.

The danger lies between generosity and suddenness. You give openly and for a long time fail to notice an imbalance: hope explains away any inequality as a temporary difficulty. The account builds up in silence — and then everything collapses at once. For the other person this can come as a complete surprise: yesterday you were there for them, today it is “we’re finished”. After a collapse like that it is hard to open up again, and the next person gets less light than they might have — paying for someone else’s debts.

energy_field:17-9-8.heading: Shining for others, refuelling in silence
paragraphs: Sharing comes naturally to you. The Star shows in the way you act: time, advice and skills are given generously, as if water were pouring from a jug, and that is the kind of work you do best. But the water in that jug is refilled in silence. The Hermit explains where your strength comes from: from hours alone, a road of your own, an inner lantern by whose light you work out what is what. And Justice governs your feelings: you are at peace when the exchange is fair and everyone receives according to their deeds.

**You shine for others precisely because you keep coming back to your own light.** For example, all day you explain, help and answer colleagues’ questions. And in the evening you need quiet — a walk without headphones, a book, no conversations. By morning you are ready to give again, and you give generously, but without strain. The people close to you who understand this rhythm receive warm, clear-headed attention from you.

Things get hard when solitude is taken for coldness and generosity for a duty. You have given a lot, but no one has left you any quiet: the evening is again taken up with other people’s requests, and saying no feels unfair to those who are waiting. Inside grows a sense of an unfair exchange: you shine, but you aren’t allowed to refuel. Resentment builds up in silence, and one day you withdraw into yourself for a long time — not to rest, but to wall yourself off. Then the people close to you lose both your generosity and your warmth at once.

energy_field:17-11-1.heading: Inspiring and getting straight to work
paragraphs: There is a lot of light in your overall tone. The Star shows in your affairs: you act openly and generously, and you gladly put yourself into whatever brings benefit and hope to others. Strength governs your energy: it comes from calm composure — the ability to deal gently with your own fears and outbursts without wasting yourself on a fight. And in your feelings the Magician leads: the brightest feeling comes when an idea turns into a result thanks to your own hands and mind.

**You don’t just cheer people on — you show that hope can be made real.** Say your neighbours have long dreamed of a playground in the courtyard. While everyone else sighs, you calmly collect signatures, find a contractor, sort it out with the housing association. A couple of months later children are already on the swings, and you feel that special joy of something coming together because you found a way to do it.

The vulnerable spot is other people’s troubles that you can’t solve. Generosity pulls you to help, composure lets you keep going for a long time, and satisfaction comes only when you have influenced the outcome. But when the outcome doesn’t depend on you — someone else’s heavy loss, a decision a person has to make alone — confusion rises inside: you are there, but there is nothing to do. And then you take on anything at all just to be acting, though sometimes a person simply needs you to be there.

energy_field:17-11-10.heading: Waiting out the bottom of the wheel
captions: Back to work after a slump
paragraphs: You tend to believe that a rise will follow a fall. The Star sets the rhythm of your affairs: you act with open hope, return to work quickly after a hard stretch and gladly share what you have. Strength explains where your energy comes from: from a gentle self-possession that doesn’t let panic take over. And the Wheel of Fortune sounds in your feelings: your mood clearly follows the course of events — success gives you wings, failure bows you down, and you know this about yourself.

**You know how to wait out the bottom of the wheel without losing your light.** Say a year turns out to be hard: the orders dry up, plans fall through. You admit that this is a low point and don’t pretend to be cheerful — but you don’t sink into despair either. You do the little that can be done and support those who have it even harder. And when the wheel turns, you are the first to be ready, because all that time you never put out your hope.

The flip side is a habit of waiting for the turn instead of looking for it. If you always believe that “it’ll pass soon”, you can stand still for too long: patiently, calmly, hopefully. The wheel really does turn, but not necessarily in the direction you need. And when the rise is slow to come, calm gives way to weariness, and hope to a quiet grudge against fate — although fate never promised anything.

energy_field:17-12-11.heading: Giving generously and knowing when to stop
captions: A new view after a pause
paragraphs: Sometimes the best way to help is to stop for a while. The Star shows in your affairs: time, hands and attention are given generously, without long calculation, and work goes best when someone needs it. The Hanged Man explains how your strength works: it comes back during a pause, when you step out of the bustle and look at everything from a different angle. And your feelings pass through Strength: you meet strong emotions, your own and other people’s, calmly and with quiet courage.

**Your generosity doesn’t run dry because you know how to stop in time and look at things differently.** Say for several months you have been helping a friend through a difficult divorce: talks, a house move, paperwork. At some point you are running on empty — and instead of playing the hero, you take a couple of days’ break. You come back with a fresh view: what he needs now is not looking after but faith that he will manage on his own. And that change helps you both.

The risk is a pause that becomes a way of life. Putting your own plans aside for someone else comes so naturally that whole years get put aside: a trip, a course of study, a business of your own — “when it’s possible”. Calm composure helps you not notice the cost: you don’t complain, you don’t snap, you keep everything in hand. But light that is given without return eventually dims. And it turns out that you are hanging upside down not for the sake of a new view, but simply out of habit.

energy_field:18-8-17.heading: Finding your way through fog by a star
paragraphs: Your undertakings often begin in uncertainty. The Moon sets your material rhythm: you move by instinct, feeling your way, and you can’t always explain why you chose this particular road. Justice governs your strength: clarity brings it back — when facts can be separated from impressions, weighed up and honestly named for what they are. And in your feelings the Star shines: even in a murky period there is hope ahead, and after a hard stage comes a sense of inner renewal.

**You let yourself walk into the unknown, but you check your route against the facts — and you don’t lose hope.** Say you move to a city where you don’t know anyone. The first decisions — where to live, what to take on — are made almost blindly, by feel. But every week you honestly take stock: what has been confirmed, what turned out to be an illusion. Little by little the fog lifts, and every new landmark is as welcome as a star in a break in the clouds.

It gets harder when the scales have nothing to rest on and imagination is only too happy to fill in. In a murky situation — someone’s silence, unclear conditions at work — the Moon will draw in what is missing, and the need for clarity will push you to reach a verdict based on those guesses. Hope, meanwhile, tips the scales towards the better version: “they’re just busy”, “it’ll all work out”. The decision looks well weighed, but what lay on the scales were not facts but moonlit reflections. And when the fog clears, the disappointment hits harder than an honest “I don’t know yet” would have.
